n: John the Baptist and the Father announced Jesus as the Messiah ({{Matthew 3:13-17|3:13–17}}). He then endured testing in the wilderness with obedience ({{Matthew 4:1-11|4:1–11}}). After this, the Messiah was ready to begin his work. He first preached the message of the kingdom of God to the people of Galilee.

Jesus expands his ministry (see {{Matthew 4:23-9:34|Matthew 4:23–9:34}}) by sending his disciples to other people in Israel ({{Matthew 10:5-6|10:5–6}}). The instructions Jesus gives his disciples ({{Matthew 10:5-42|10:5–42}}) emphasizes missionary work and the opposition and challenges they will encounter.

John the Baptist had questions about who Jesus was. Jesus answered John’s questions by using words from a prophecy in Isaiah 35:5–6. This was a prophecy about Jesus.

Jesus was the one through whom God was healing and setting his people free. Jesus called Israel to turn away from sin and repent. It wasn’t yet the time for judgement. It was time to heal and to preach the good news of God’s kingdom.

Jesus then explained that John was a messenger. He was the messenger like Elijah whom God had promised to send (Malachi 4:5–6). But not everyone in Israel accepted Jesus and John.

- Herod Antipas arrested John ({{Matthew 4:12|Matthew 4:12}}) because John criticized Herod's immoral relationship with Herodias, the wife of his half-brother ({{Matthew 14:1-12|14:1–12}}). 

- *the works of Christ*: These actions showed that Jesus is the Messiah (Christ) ({{Matthew 8:1-9:34|8:1–9:34}}).

This section starts with John the Baptist’s doubt. It ends by honoring his faith and his work ({{Matthew 11:7-19|Matthew 11:7–19}}). The people's rejection of John ({{Matthew 11:16-19|11:16–19}}) hints at their future rejection of Jesus.

This section focuses on two main reactions to Jesus: acceptance and rejection. The first part ({{Matthew 11:2-12:50|Matthew 11:2–12:50}}) shows Jewish leaders rejecting Jesus, while his disciples are learning to understand and accept him.

The miracles of compassion that Jesus did showed that the kingdom of God had begun (see {{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}; {{Isaiah 29:18-19|Isaiah 29:18–19}}; {{Isaiah 35:5-6|35:5–6}}; {{Isaiah 61:1|61:1}}). Jesus expected John to realize he was fulfilling Old Testament prophecies.

*Who does not fall away on account of Me*: Jesus intended that the works mentioned in {{Matthew 11:5|verse 5}} were meant to help John the Baptist and his disciples decide about Jesus. But Jesus knew that some unexpected parts of his ministry would cause people to reject him.
*A reed swaying in the wind*: This refers to an unstable person. The implied answer to this rhetorical question is "no."

John the Baptist was the greatest person ever to have lived. Yet the least of the followers of Jesus are greater than John because they live in the new covenant of salvation through Jesus (see {{Matthew 4:17|4:17}}). The new covenant refers to God's new agreement with people that came through Jesus. Salvation (being saved from sin and its consequences) comes through death and resurrection of Jesus.

- *The kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence*: The Greek verb can mean either that the kingdom suffers violence (negative) or that it forcefully advances (positive). In {{Luke 16:16|Luke 16:16}}, a different verb (“preached”) makes the statement clearly positive.

- *the violent lay claim to it*: This phrase can also have either a negative or positive sense. Negatively, it may point to those who opposed John (see {{Matthew 11:2|Matthew 11:2}}; {{Matthew 14:1-12|14:1–12}}) and persecuted the kingdom’s messengers. Positively, it may refer to people “forcing their way in” (see {{Luke 16:16|Luke 16:16}}), urgently pressing into the kingdom through radical trust and obedience.
*He is the Elijah who was to come: *John fulfills the Old Testament prophecy about the prophet Elijah's return ({{Matthew 17:10-13|Matthew 17:10–13}}; see {{Malachi 4:5|Malachi 4:5}}).

John’s message was like funeral songs. He lived with strict self-denial, fasting often and not drinking wine ({{Matthew 11:18|Matthew 11:18}}; see {{Matthew 3:4|3:4}}). The message of Jesus is more like wedding songs, with feasting and drinking (see {{Matthew 9:9-17|9:9–17}}). In both cases, the people of this time respond to God's messenger with indifference and rejection.

Here Jesus describes how both John and he himself offended the people of that generation.

John lived in the wilderness, eating locusts and honey ({{Matthew 3:1|Matthew 3:1}}, {{Matthew 3:4|4}}). People accused him of having a demon. 

Jesus, by contrast, ate and drank freely with others. People accused him of being like a rebellious son (see {{Deuteronomy 21:18-21|Deuteronomy 21:18–21}}).

The miracles Jesus performed showed he was the Messiah ({{Matthew 11:5-6|Matthew 11:5–6}}). These miracles demanded people to repent ({{Matthew 11:20|11:20}}). Those who rejected the Messiah faced great judgment, because Jesus had clearly shown who he is.

God was working among the people of Israel through Jesus. Yet they didn’t accept Jesus and his message of good news.

Jesus warned them about what would happen if they continued to say no to God. He talked about cities from long ago that were famous for evil deeds. The people who had lived in those cities never saw Jesus’ powerful signs. Jesus said that if they had, they would have turned away from their sin.

Yet the Jewish cities in Galilee weren’t turning away from sin and towards God. Jesus wanted people to really know God as their Father. He saw that religious duties were like heavy loads that people carried around.

Following and serving Jesus gives people rest. He invited all people to his way of rest and peace.

As Jesus traveled through the villages of Galilee (Korazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum) he revealed more of himself to the people. Because of this greater revelation, their refusal to listen brought a more severe judgment. Jesus compared their judgment to that of the pagan cities Tyre ({{Isaiah 23:1-18|Isaiah 23}}; {{Ezekiel 26:1-28:19|Ezekiel 26:1–28:19}}), Sidon ({{Ezekiel 28:20-23|Ezekiel 28:20–23}}), and Sodom ({{Genesis 18:22-19:29|Genesis 18:22–19:29}}).
*Hades:* This is the Greek equivalent to the Hebrew term *Sheol* (see study note on Psalm 6:5).

*The wise and learned*: The Pharisees and teachers of religious law thought their access to God was guaranteed through their knowledge and practice of the law. The disciples of Jesus were more childlike (see {{Matthew 21:15-16|Matthew 21:15–16}}).
This passage is about the small group of people who accept the Messiah and follow his teachings, even though most of their generation does not.

Jesus showed his close relationship with the Father. Everything he said and did came from his unity with his Father (see {{John 10:14-15|John 10:14–15}}; {{John 14:6-7|14:6–7}}; {{John 15:23-24|15:23–24}}; {{John 16:15|16:15}}; {{John 17:25-26|17:25–26}}).

- The heavy burdens were probably caused by the legal demands of the religious teachers and Pharisees (see {{Matthew 23:4|Matthew 23:4}}). 

- *rest*: This means spiritual refreshment, either now or in the future (compare {{Matthew 1:21|1:21}}; {{Hebrews 4:8-11|Hebrews 4:8–11}}).

A *yoke*, which connects two animals, symbolizes the demands of being a disciple of Jesus. Unlike the "yoke" of religious leaders, the yoke of Jesus is *easy* and *light*. This is not because it demands less of a person (see {{Matthew 7:13-14|7:13–14}}). But it is because the Messiah's power through the Holy Spirit makes it possible (see {{Acts 15:10|Acts 15:10}}; {{1 John 5:3|1 John 5:3}}). 

Israel's spiritual leaders imposed religious demands (see {{Matthew 23:4|Matthew 23:4}}; {{Acts 15:10|Acts 15:10}}). This included 613 Old Testament commands and added traditions. Jesus urged those burdened by the Pharisees' rules to come to him (see {{Matthew 11:28|Matthew 11:28}}) to find the salvation for which they deeply longed. This call to salvation involves living obediently to the new teachings of Jesus. Jesus invites people to build a relationship with a humble and gentle teacher.

*The Sabbath *was the seventh day of the week. God intended it to be a day of complete rest according to Old Testament laws ({{Genesis 2:2-3|Genesis 2:2–3}}; {{Exodus 20:8-11|Exodus 20:8–11}}). Christ fulfills the Sabbath (compare {{Hebrews 4:1-11|Hebrews 4:1–11}}).
This exchange shows the Pharisees' lack of compassion as they placed a heavy burden on others ({{Matthew 11:29-30|Matthew 11:29–30}}).

Jesus’ disciples broke off some ears of corn and ate them on the Sabbath day. The Pharisees complained about this to Jesus. They accused the disciples of breaking the laws about the Sabbath day.

Jesus reminded them that David broke those laws when he was hungry. Priests also broke those laws every Sabbath day when they worked in the temple. Jesus was claiming that he had the same rights as King David. And his work was more important than the priests’ work in the temple.

Then Jesus healed a man on the Sabbath day. The Pharisees didn’t want him to do this. But Jesus wouldn’t stop doing God’s work just because some people opposed him. The Pharisees then started making plans to kill Jesus.

Matthew closely connects the offer of rest Jesus gives ({{Matthew 11:28-30|Matthew 11:28–30}}) with a discussion about the Sabbath. The rest Jesus offers liberates people from human traditions about the Sabbath (see {{Hebrews 4:1-11|Hebrews 4:1–11}}). The Pharisees rejected Jesus because they had a commitment to their tradition.
Sometimes it was right to suspend ceremonial laws ({{1 Samuel 21:1-6|1 Samuel 21:1–6}}).
The Pharisees did not understand that God designed the Sabbath to benefit people. They made it a heavy burden instead.

Priests worked on the Sabbath ({{Leviticus 24:8-9|Leviticus 24:8–9}}; {{Numbers 28:9-10|Numbers 28:9–10}}), and the Pharisees did not find this offensive. If the priests’ work for the temple on the Sabbath is allowed, then certainly Jesus can do the same because he is greater than the temple (see {{Matthew 4:23|Matthew 4:23}}; {{Matthew 9:35|9:35}}; {{Matthew 11:2-6|11:2–6}}, {{Matthew 11:20-30|20–30}}).
The Pharisees misunderstood the meaning of the Sabbath. Their view went against Scripture because it ignored the greater principle of mercy.
Jesus is greater than King David, the priests, and the temple. He also rules over the Sabbath.
*their synagogue*: A separation was developing between Jesus and Judaism (also {{Matthew 4:23|Matthew 4:23}}).
This second Sabbath controversy criticizes the Pharisees for prioritizing rules over people's needs (see {{Matthew 12:7|Matthew 12:7}}, {{Matthew 12:11-12|11–12}}).

*Is it lawful*: Jewish teachers of the law said healing on the Sabbath was allowed only if someone’s life was in danger. Because the person’s life was not in danger, the Pharisees believed that healing was not allowed.
They rescued animals but ignored people, which was inconsistent.

Many years before, God made a promise recorded in the book of the prophet Isaiah. This promise was a prophecy.

Matthew showed that Jesus’ actions fulfilled that prophecy. Jesus was the servant God sent into the world. He spoke and worked for justice. He was tender towards those who were hurting. He encouraged those who had been harmed.

He would bring what is good, right and true to all nations.
This summary of the ministry of Jesus explains that Jesus is the Messiah, God's servant who will bring salvation to all nations (see {{Isaiah 42:1-4|Isaiah 42:1–4}}).

- This quote is similar to the story of the baptism of Jesus ({{Matthew 3:13-17|Matthew 3:13–17}}). 

- *Justice* (or *judgment*): This can be good or bad. Here, it probably means something positive ({{Matthew 12:20|12:20}}; compare {{Matthew 23:23|23:23}}).

Jesus does not add to people’s spiritual burdens. Instead, he gives them forgiveness with compassion and the sustenance (nourishment and strength) they need (see {{Matthew 11:28-30|Matthew 11:28–30}}; {{Matthew 12:1-14|12:1–14}}).

Jesus healed a man who couldn’t see or speak. Jesus also drove demons out of him. The Pharisees claimed that Jesus used the power of the devil to do this. People who said that the devil gave Jesus power were speaking evil against God’s Spirit.

Jesus wanted people to understand that good deeds and evil deeds come from the heart. He used a tree to explain what he meant. He said good deeds are like good fruit. A good tree produces good fruit. Bad deeds are like bad fruit. A bad tree produces bad fruit. The way people act shows what is inside their heart.

Jesus came to rescue people from sin and to give them hearts that love God.
The Pharisees, the teachers of religious law, and many people of his generation rejected the Messiah.

- People were amazed by the miracles Jesus performed ({{Mark 2:12|Mark 2:12}}; {{Mark 6:51|6:51}}; {{Luke 2:47|Luke 2:47}}; {{Luke 8:56|8:56}}; {{Luke 24:22|24:22}}). 

- *Could this be:* The question expected a negative answer. Jesus did not fit their idea of the Messiah, but his miracles made them wonder.
Jesus said in essence, “If I drive out demons by the power of Satan, then Satan is fighting against his own kingdom. That would be foolish for him to do.”

*your sons*: Jesus forced them to think consistently. If Satan's power casts out demons, then the disciples of the Pharisees were just as guilty, since they too cast out demons (see {{Acts 19:13-16|Acts 19:13–16}}).

The Pharisees were confronted with the kingdom of God and chose to reject it (see {{Luke 17:20-21|Luke 17:20–21}}; {{1 John 3:8|1 John 3:8}}). Through his miracles, Jesus showed the power of the kingdom in the present world. But the kingdom will reach its full completion when Christ comes again.

- This parable forced the Pharisees to answer a simple question. Can anyone drive out demons without first controlling Satan's powers and opposing him (see {{Isaiah 49:24-26|Isaiah 49:24–26}}; {{Isaiah 53:12|53:12}})? 

- *ties up the strong man*: This points to how Jesus defeated Satan. He overcame him in the wilderness temptation ({{Matthew 4:1-11|Matthew 4:1–11}}), continued to overcome him throughout his ministry (see {{Luke 10:17-20|Luke 10:17–20}}), and won the final victory at the cross (see {{Colossians 2:14-15|Colossians 2:14–15}}).

The Pharisees accused Jesus of being under the influence of Satan. Jesus explained that he, as the Messiah, cast out demons through the power of the Holy Spirit. In this context, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit can only mean attributing the ministry and exorcisms of Jesus to Satan’s power.

God can forgive people who are confused about Jesus calling himself the "Son of Man." But, God will not forgive a person that says the Holy Spirit's work comes from Satan. Today, this is like completely rejecting the conviction of the Holy Spirit about Jesus. This refers to when an unbeliever ultimately rejects the good news about Jesus (see {{Hebrews 6:4-6|Hebrews 6:4–6}}; {{1 John 5:16-21|1 John 5:16–21}}).
Jesus addressed the main issue. The Pharisees did not accept him or believe his work came from God because they were wicked (see {{Matthew 7:15-27|7:15–27}}).

- The *careless word*, in this context, was the claim that demons empowered Jesus. 

- What a person says will either free or condemn them on the day of judgment. What people say shows the true state of their hearts.

*See a sign*: People expected the Messiah to perform amazing miracles. This expectation was probably inspired by stories about Moses ({{Exodus 4:1-9|Exodus 4:1–9}}; see also {{Isaiah 7:11|Isaiah 7:11}}, {{Isaiah 7:14|14}}; {{Isaiah 38:7-8|38:7–8}}). They believed the Messiah would show these miracles on demand (see {{Matthew 16:1-4|Matthew 16:1–4}}; {{Luke 23:8|Luke 23:8}}; {{John 2:18|John 2:18}}; {{John 4:48|4:48}}; {{John 6:30|6:30}}; {{John 7:31|7:31}}; {{John 9:16|9:16}}; {{John 11:47|11:47}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:22|1 Corinthians 1:22}}).

Jesus had done many mighty works of healing throughout Israel. Some religious leaders asked Jesus for one more sign. But they had already decided that they didn’t believe in Jesus or want to follow him.

Jesus’ sign would be like the sign in the story about Jonah. Jonah spent three days and nights inside a huge fish. Then he came back out and preached God’s message. Something like this would happen to Jesus. Jesus would be dead for three days. Then he would be raised from the dead and come out of the grave.

Jesus’ message about God’s kingdom is greater than Jonah’s message. It’s even greater than Solomon’s wisdom. Jesus explained what would happen to those who didn’t believe his message. They would be found guilty on judgement day. Yet everyone who does believe in him and who obeys God is part of his family.

- To demand a sign shows a lack of faith. 

- The sign of the prophet Jonah was his "resurrection" from the large fish after three days and nights. It also referred to his preaching ({{Matthew 12:41|12:41}}; {{Luke 11:32|Luke 11:32}}). This was similar to the burial, resurrection, and preaching of Jesus. Jesus compared Jonah's experience to what he would experience. He was not predicting the exact timing of his death and resurrection. 

- *Heart of the earth* is another way of saying "the grave."

*One greater*: Jesus is greater than the temple ({{Matthew 12:6|Matthew 12:6}}), the prophet Jonah, and King Solomon. So, rejecting him brings more severe judgment on this "wicked and adulterous generation" ({{Matthew 12:39|12:39}}).
*The Queen of the South*: see {{1 Kings 10:1-13|1 Kings 10:1–13.}}
People believed demons liked the dry desert (see {{Revelation 18:2|Revelation 18:2}}; compare {{Isaiah 13:21|Isaiah 13:21}}; {{Isaiah 34:14|34:14}}).

The Messiah came in victory over evil spirits. But instead of turning back to God, the nation as a whole rejected him. Jesus said that when an evil spirit is cast out, it may return if the person is not ready to resist it. In the same way, judgment would come on this evil generation because they rejected the Messiah (God’s chosen one).

Those who are true members in the family of Jesus obey the will of God. They show this obedience by obeying the commands of Jesus (see {{Matthew 7:21|Matthew 7:21}}). Obedience does not earn entrance into this family, but a person cannot be a member of this family if they do not obey him (see {{Matthew 3:15|3:15}}; {{Matthew 5:17-48|5:17–48}}; {{Matthew 6:10|6:10}}, {{Matthew 6:12|12}}; {{Matthew 7:13-27|7:13–27}}; {{Matthew 21:31|21:31}}).

When Jesus first began his work among the people of Israel, he spoke openly. He announced the kingdom of heaven and invited people to be part of it. But the religious leaders refused to accept his teaching. And many people in Israel doubted that Jesus really was the Messiah.

Because of this, Jesus changed the way he taught in Israel. He stopped speaking plainly and instead taught by telling stories called parables. This was the start of Jesus’ third long message. It was full of parables about God’s kingdom.

Jesus told the story about seeds in public to everyone. But he only explained it in private to his disciples. He explained that many people hear the message about the kingdom. Many of them refuse to understand it. Others hear Jesus’ message and obey him. They are like seeds that produce a good crop. Words and actions that accomplish what God wants are the good crop.

In the third major speech recorded by Matthew (see study note on Matthew 5:1–7:29), Jesus here recognized the separation of his followers from others ({{Matthew 13:14|Matthew 13:14}}, {{Matthew 13:16|16}}). He began to reveal the secrets of the kingdom of heaven privately to them through parables.

- This parable (explained in {{Matthew 13:18-23|Matthew 13:18–23}}) discusses the mostly negative reactions of the Jewish people to Jesus and his message. 

- *Parables* (Greek *parabolē*): These are stories that use everyday life to explain a spiritual truth. To understand a parable, find the main comparison (analogy) and consider its historical and gospel context. Then a person can understand the main message. Avoid finding unintended symbolic meanings in every part of a parable.

- From this point on, Jesus rarely taught the general public. Instead, he focused on teaching those who had committed themselves to him ({{Matthew 13:1-20:34|Matthew 13:1–20:34}}). But he would once again confront Israel ({{Matthew 21:1-23:39|21:1–23:39}}). 

- *The people* were the unbelieving opponents mentioned again in {{Matthew 13:11|13:11}} (“them”) and {{Matthew 13:12|13:12}} (“whoever does not have”).

- *The knowledge … has been given to you:* God allowed the disciples to understand the importance of Jesus. God also allowed them to respond to the message of Jesus about the kingdom of heaven with faith and obedience (see {{Matthew 13:19|13:19}}, {{Matthew 13:23|23}}). 

- *the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven*: Salvation is available through Jesus as the fulfillment of Old Testament promises.
Jesus answered the disciples question in {{Matthew 13:10|verse 10}}. He told them that the Jews' stubborn disbelief and rejection of him brought God's condemnation.

- Jesus told parables, and those who believed him understood them. Yet, those who rejected Jesus found that his parables increased their disbelief. 

- *Though seeing, they do not see … hear or understand:* They lacked the faith to recognize the truth ({{Matthew 13:19|Matthew 13:19}}, {{Matthew 13:23|23}}) and respond ({{Mark 8:18|Mark 8:18}}; {{John 12:40|John 12:40}}; see also {{Jeremiah 5:21|Jeremiah 5:21}}).

Similar to the message of the prophet Isaiah, the message of Jesus has two effects:

- It judges those who do not believe or obey, and 

- it creates a small group of faithful people who do the Lord's will ({{Matthew 21:43|Matthew 21:43}}).

Jesus fulfilled what the prophets and Old Testament believers wanted to see and hear. He fulfills the Old Testament promises (see {{Isaiah 52:15|Isaiah 52:15}}; {{John 8:56|John 8:56}}; {{1 Peter 1:10|1 Peter 1:10}}).
*Does not understand it*: Responding to God's message directly relates to understanding its importance.

*Has no root, he remains for only a season*: The issue is a lack of enduring faith and obedience (see {{Matthew 7:13-27|Matthew 7:13–27}}; {{Matthew 10:22|10:22}}), especially when confronted by persecution.

Jesus talked about the competing demands in life (see also {{Matthew 8:18-22|Matthew 8:18–22}}). The worries of life can become overwhelming and lead people away from faithful obedience (see {{Matthew 6:19-34|6:19–34}}). The temptation of wealth, especially its deceptive nature, is a common theme in Matthew (for example, {{Matthew 4:8-10|4:8–10}}; {{Matthew 6:24|6:24}}; {{Matthew 13:44-45|13:44–45}}). God values faith, obedience, and helping those in need more than wealth (for example, {{Matthew 19:21|19:21}}; {{Matthew 25:31-46|25:31–46}}).
*Produces a crop*: This probably refers to faithfully obeying the commands of Jesus (for example, {{Matthew 5:1-7:27|Matthew 5:1–7:27}}; {{Matthew 28:20|28:20}}).

Jesus’ stories taught about his work and the coming of the kingdom of heaven. Jesus’ work on earth didn’t stop evil everywhere all at once. Evil is allowed to remain along with God’s kingdom for now.

Later, judgement will come and evil will be destroyed. God’s kingdom starts in small ways. It grows and spreads through the whole world. All nations and all peoples can be part of it.

This way of understanding God’s kingdom is like a treasure. Some people recognise that Jesus is from God. They understand that his work brings God’s kingdom to earth. These people understand the value of this treasure.
*Weeds*, also known as *tares* or bearded darnel, look a lot like wheat. Farmers waited until the plants grew to tell them apart. Intentionally contaminating crops like this was against the law.

Jesus rebuked the sons of Zebedee for wanting to destroy villages that did not believe in him ({{Luke 9:54-55|Luke 9:54–55}}). He told his disciples not to seek revenge against enemies. Judgment is God's responsibility (see {{Matthew 7:1-5|Matthew 7:1–5}}). Jesus urges his disciples to wait patiently for God's righteous judgment ("the harvest"; see {{Luke 13:6-9|Luke 13:6–9}}).

Jesus used surprising and vivid images in these parables. He probably wanted to show how the kingdom of Heaven would grow through preaching the good news. More probably, he wanted to highlight the contrast between small beginnings and a glorious end. He also encouraged the disciples to be patient (see also {{Matthew 16:24-17:13|Matthew 16:24–17:13}}).

Usually, yeast refers to the influence of evil (for example, {{Matthew 16:6|16:6}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:6|1 Corinthians 5:6}}; {{Galatians 5:9|Galatians 5:9}}). But in this context it represents the positive and widespread influence of the kingdom of Heaven.

Even the way Jesus taught fulfilled prophecies from the Old Testament. {{Psalm 78:2-3|Psalm 78:2–3}} talks about sharing the history of God's revelation with future generations. What Jesus revealed in his teachings are the most important part of that history ({{Matthew 13:10-17|Matthew 13:10–17}}; {{1 Corinthians 2:7|1 Corinthians 2:7}}).

- They *went into the house* (see {{Matthew 13:1|Matthew 13:1}}). Jesus taught in public using parables, but he explained their meanings privately to his disciples. 

- *Explain*: The disciples had the special opportunity to learn the secrets of the kingdom ({{Matthew 13:11-17|13:11–17}}). But they did not understand the parables until Jesus explained them.

These verses explain the parable from {{Matthew 13:24-30|Matthew 13:24–30}}. The people of the kingdom (like wheat) live side by side with those who do not belong to it (like weeds). The “field” is the world, and this will continue until the end of history. 

The mystery of the kingdom is that it is already present in the world, but God has not yet removed the wicked in judgment. The disciples of Jesus must learn patience and trust God’s timing.

- *The field is the world*: The kingdom of heaven includes all nations ({{Matthew 28:16-20|Matthew 28:16–20}}). 

- The* sons of the kingdom* are those who obey Jesus ({{Matthew 13:11-17|13:11–17}}, {{Matthew 13:23|23}}; {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}).
The harvest of judgment, which began with the first coming of the Son of Man ({{Matthew 3:12|Matthew 3:12}}) will be completed when he returns ({{Revelation 14:14-16|Revelation 14:14–16}}).
*His kingdom*: The rule of the Son of Man will be visible over everything at the "end of the age" ({{Matthew 13:40|Matthew 13:40}}).
The righteous people will obey God's will as Jesus showed, unlike those "who practice lawlessness" ({{Matthew 13:41|Matthew 13:41}}).

- *Treasure hidden in a field*: People buried treasures to protect them from thieves and military enemies ({{Matthew 25:25|Matthew 25:25}}). 

- *in his joy*: Those who find the kingdom of heaven experience more joy from it than any temporary pleasure can offer (see {{1 Peter 1:8|1 Peter 1:8}}).

Another mystery of the kingdom of heaven ({{Matthew 13:11|13:11}}) is that it is more valuable than any treasure. So, a person should give up everything to get it (see {{Matthew 19:21|19:21}}, {{Matthew 19:29|29}}; {{Philippians 3:7|Philippians 3:7}}).

This parable is about God's judgment on the last day ({{Matthew 25:31-46|Matthew 25:31–46}}). Then he will forever separate the wicked from the righteous. This warning emphasizes the importance of the two earlier invitations to make a decision to trust Jesus.

The wicked are people who do not obey God's will revealed by Jesus. The righteous are those who obey God's will (see {{Matthew 5:21-48|Matthew 5:21–48}}; {{Matthew 6:1|6:1}}, {{Matthew 6:33|33}}; {{Matthew 7:13-27|7:13–27}}; {{Matthew 12:33-37|12:33–37}}; {{Matthew 16:27|16:27}}).
Understanding the secrets of the kingdom of heaven is a gift from God ({{Matthew 13:10-17|Matthew 13:10–17}}, {{Matthew 13:23|23}}).

- A teacher of religious law who becomes a disciple in the kingdom of God changes allegiance. He now looks to Jesus as the way of salvation.

- *new treasures as well as old*: This order shows that the new covenant brought by Jesus takes first place. It is greater than the old covenant that God gave through Abraham and Moses ({{Matthew 5:17-20|Matthew 5:17–20}}; {{Matthew 19:16-22|19:16–22}}).

People in Jesus’ hometown didn’t understand how Jesus had so much wisdom. They didn’t understand how he had power to do miracles. They were angry about Jesus and refused to believe that he came from God.

At the same time, Jewish and Roman leaders were angry at John the Baptist. John had spoken against Herod Antipas for being unfaithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. Herod put John in prison and later had John’s head cut off.

Both John and Jesus were treated without honour or respect for sharing God’s message.

That Jesus was rejected at home is part of the ongoing theme of the Messiah’s rejection by his own people (see chapter {{Matthew 12:1-50|Matthew 12}}; {{Matthew 15:1-20|15:1–20}}; {{Matthew 16:1-12|16:1–12}}).
*carpenter’s son*: a carpenter (literally, *craftsman*) worked with his hands in wood, metal, or stone.
They felt very insulted. Focusing on the ordinary social status of Jesus ({{John 6:42|John 6:42}}), they missed his unique importance.
To understand the message of Jesus ({{Matthew 13:10-17|13:10–17}}) and experience his miracles, you need faith.

Herod Antipas’s official title was *tetrarch*, which means a ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom. He ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39 (see {{Matthew 2:19-22|Matthew 2:19–22}}). Jesus called Antipas “that fox” ({{Luke 13:32|Luke 13:32}}). John the Baptist rightly condemned him for adultery ({{Matthew 14:3-12|Matthew 14:3–12}}; {{Luke 3:19-20|Luke 3:19–20}}).
People were saying that John had been resurrected from the dead (see {{Matthew 16:14|16:14}}).

John the Baptist’s message drew large crowds, which leaders saw as a political threat (see Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.5.2). Years after John was executed, many Jews believed that Herod’s military defeat by King Aretas in AD 36 was God’s judgment for killing an innocent man.
John kept warning Herod about his sin (see {{Leviticus 18:6|Leviticus 18:6}}; {{Leviticus 20:21|20:21}}).
Herodias's daughter was probably Salome. She would have come from Herodias' earlier marriage to Philip. Such sexually suggestive dances were common among corrupt royalty.
Herod Antipas often made extravagant and foolish promises.
In ancient times, presenting a head on a tray was a known practice (see Josephus, *Antiquities* 13.4.8; 14.15.13; 18.5.1; 20.5.1).

When Jesus heard about John the Baptist’s death, he wanted to be alone. But the crowds found him and surrounded him.

Jesus cared deeply for the people. He healed those who were ill. Then he fed them. He did this by using the small amount of food that the disciples had.

The disciples had only five loaves and two fish to offer. Jesus made it enough to feed over 5,000 people. This was the first of two miracles about feeding people recorded by Matthew.

It showed something about God’s kingdom. God’s kingdom grows when God’s people are willing to freely give what they have. It doesn’t matter how small the gift is.

What Jesus did consistently fulfilled Old Testament promises about the kingdom of heaven and the Messiah ({{Matthew 11:5-6|Matthew 11:5–6}}; {{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}). Here, Jesus reminded people of God's gift of *manna* to the Israelites ({{Exodus 16:1-36|Exodus 16}}; see {{John 6:32|John 6:32}}). This showed that he is the promised prophet of the end times (see {{Deuteronomy 18:15-16|Deuteronomy 18:15–16}}).
*About five thousand men were fed, in addition to women and children*: At that time, they counted families by the heads of households, not each person.
After Jesus miraculously fed the crowd, they wanted to make him king ({{John 6:15|John 6:15}}). He withdrew from the crowd because it was not the right time.

Jesus showed his power over nature, giving the disciples a chance to trust him as the Son of God ({{Matthew 14:33|Mathhew 14:33}}; see also {{Matthew 8:23-27|8:23–27}}; {{Psalm 8:6|Psalm 8:6}}; {{Hebrews 2:8-9|Hebrews 2:8–9}}).

Jesus sent the crowd and his disciples away so that he could be alone. He wanted to pray.

When Jesus walked on the water the disciples saw his authority over nature. This scared them. Jesus spoke comforting words to them.

Peter had faith to follow Jesus on the water at first. When Peter became scared, Jesus saved him from sinking.

Then Jesus continued to show his authority over nature and illness as he healed people. His power is so strong that people were healed even by touching his clothes.

Jesus often went to quiet places to pray, especially during important times in his life and work ({{Matthew 26:36-46|Matthew 26:36–46}}; {{Mark 1:35|Mark 1:35}}; {{Luke 5:16|Luke 5:16}}; {{Luke 6:12|6:12}}; {{Luke 9:28|9:28}}).

- *During the fourth watch of the night: *This was between 3:00 and 6:00 am by Roman timekeeping. 

- *Jesus went out … walking on the sea: *This act showed God’s rule over the stormy sea (see {{Job 9:8|Job 9:8}}; {{Psalm 77:19|Psalm 77:19}}; {{Isaiah 43:16|Isaiah 43:16}}).
*It is I (*literally *I am*): This statement is associated with the appearance of God himself (see also {{John 8:24|John 8:24}}; {{John 18:5-6|18:5–6}}; compare {{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}).
To understand why Jesus performed miracles, refer to the study notes on Matthew 11:5 and 12:28.
The temple was in Jerusalem, which made it the center of authority in Judaism. This gave these ambassadors from the Pharisees and scribes more influence in their discussions with Jesus.

The Pharisees asked Jesus why his disciples didn’t obey the teachings of the elders. Jesus asked them why they didn’t obey God’s command to honour their mother and father.

Jesus made it clear that obeying God’s word is what mattered. It’s more important than obeying the teachings and practices of human beings.

Jesus taught what the laws about being clean really meant. What made someone unclean wasn’t what they ate. It wasn’t whether they washed their hands or not. Being unclean comes from inside a person. Evil words and actions come from someone’s heart.
Jesus accused the Pharisees of disobeying God's law because of their focus on preserving traditions.

- Jewish teachers developed long-standing traditions to explain how the written Torah should guide daily life. These traditions were memorized and passed from teacher to student by word of mouth(see {{1 Corinthians 11:23|1 Corinthians 11:23}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:1-5|15:1–5}}). 

- *break the tradition of *… *wash their hands* (see {{Mark 7:2-4|Mark 7:2–4}}; {{Luke 11:38|Luke 11:38}}): The tradition of hand washing was seen as important. Ignoring this practice was considered disobedience to the Torah and unfaithfulness to God’s will for Israel (see {{Matthew 23:25-26|Matthew 23:25–26}}).

*A gift devoted to God*: The people would probably donate a gift like this at the temple (see {{Mark 7:11|Mark 7:11}}; see also {{Proverbs 28:24|Proverbs 28:24}}) but it served as a way to avoid financially providing for one's parents.
*Nullify*: The Pharisees valued their traditions so much that they ignored God's law, turning their devotion into sinful disrespect for God's word.

- *What enters his mouth*: Jesus may have been speaking about foods that the law did not allow (such as pork or shellfish) or food made unclean by unwashed hands ({{Matthew 15:20|Matthew 15:20}}). 

- What makes a person *defiled* also makes them unfit to be with God. Jesus moved the focus from outward rules of purity to the true purity of the heart (see {{Matthew 15:18-19|15:18–19}}; {{Matthew 23:25-26|23:25–26}}; {{Acts 10:1-48|Acts 10:1–48}}; {{Romans 14:14|Romans 14:14}}).

- A person’s words show their true character (see {{Matthew 15:18-20|Matthew 15:18–20}}; {{James 3:1-12|James 3:1–12}}).

*My heavenly Father has not planted*: These Pharisees did not belong to the true people of God (see {{Matthew 3:9-12|3:9–12}}; {{Isaiah 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1–7}}; {{Jeremiah 45:4|Jeremiah 45:4}}). God will remove them at the final judgment (see {{Matthew 3:10|Matthew 3:10}}; {{Matthew 8:12|8:12}}).

Jesus left the Jewish areas and went to the Gentile territory.

A woman who wasn’t a Jew spoke to Jesus. She called him Lord and Son of David. This showed that she recognised who Jesus really was.

She asked Jesus to heal her daughter. The woman kept begging Jesus and didn’t stop.

Jesus answered that his work was for the people of Israel. Yet the woman didn’t give up.

Jesus praised her bold faith and healed her daughter.
This encounter brings up another debated issue. It is about whether Gentiles (non-Jews) can share in the kingdom of the Messiah (see {{Matthew 8:11|Matthew 8:11}}).

- *Canaanite woman:* Matthew uses this old expression to describe the woman as a pagan. 

- *Lord, Son of David*: The woman seemed to understand that Jesus was the Messiah (see {{Matthew 1:1|Matthew 1:1}}; {{Matthew 9:27|9:27}}; {{Matthew 17:15|17:15}}; {{Matthew 20:30|20:30}}).
*Did not answer a word*: Jesus stayed silent to test the woman's faith ({{Matthew 15:28|Matthew 5:28}}; compare {{Matthew 8:24|8:24}}; {{Matthew 14:16|14:16}}).

Jews often referred to pagans as *dogs*, which were considered ceremonially unclean ({{Leviticus 11:27|Leviticus 11:27}}). When Jesus spoke to the woman, he was speaking of her condition as a Gentile. She was seen as ceremonially unclean and separated from God (see {{Matthew 7:6|Matthew 7:6}}).

- Jesus returned to an area with mostly Gentiles (non-Jews) and performed many miracles. Although God mainly sent Jesus for Israel ({{Matthew 15:21-28|Matthew 15:21–28}}), Jesus also started a new era for Gentile salvation ({{Matthew 1:3|1:3}}, {{Matthew 1:5-6|5–6}}; {{Matthew 2:1-12|2:1–12}}; {{Matthew 4:12-16|4:12–16}}; {{Matthew 8:5-13|8:5–13}}; {{Matthew 15:21-28|15:21–28}}; {{Matthew 28:16-20|28:16–20}}). 

- These healings show that God's kingdom began with the work of Jesus ({{Matthew 8:1-9:34|8:1–9:34}}; {{Matthew 11:5-6|11:5–6}}; {{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}).

- *the God of Israel*: This suggests that the crowd ({{Matthew 15:30|15:30}}) was mostly Gentile.

Back in Galilee, Jesus was once again on a mountainside surrounded by a large crowd. Many in the crowd were suffering because of illness or other problems with their bodies. Jesus had deep concern for those who needed help.

Jesus healed their bodies. Then he fed the crowd of over 4,000 people. This was the second of two miracles about feeding people recorded by Matthew.

Healing people and feeding them were signs of what life in God’s kingdom is like. When God rules completely as King, his people will no longer be hurting, needy or hungry.

The earlier feeding miracle (see {{Matthew 14:13-21|Matthew 14:13–21}}) was for the Jews. This miracle extended the blessing to the gentiles. It continues the theme found in {{Matthew 15:27|Matthew 15:27}}. By this miracle, Jesus showed that he is the true "bread of life" (see {{Matthew 16:5-12|16:5–12}}; {{John 6:1-71|John 6}}).
*Magadan* is a place whose location is unknown. It may be the same as Magdala, as some Greek manuscripts say (see also {{Mark 8:10|Mark 8:10}}).

The Sadducees and Pharisees often disagreed but they worked together to oppose Jesus.

They asked Jesus to show them a sign that proved that God had sent him. But what they really wanted was to trap him and harm him.

So Jesus warned his followers about them. The Sadducees and Pharisees taught the people of Israel things that weren’t true. They were leading the people away from obeying God.
After being welcomed among the Gentiles (non-Jews), Jesus returned to his own people. There he faced rejection again.

The leaders asked Jesus for a sign from heaven ({{Matthew 16:1|Matthew 16:1}}). Jesus made a wordplay with their request. They could read signs in the sky to predict the weather (the Greek word *ouranos* means both “sky” and “heaven”). But they failed to recognize the Messiah, even though many signs had already been given (see {{Matthew 11:1-6|11:1–6}}).
*The signs of the times* were Jesus himself and the miracles he performed (see {{Matthew 16:4|Matthew 16:4}}; {{Matthew 11:2-6|11:2–6}}; {{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}).

Jesus had shown his disciples that he is the true "bread of life" ({{Matthew 15:32-39|15:32–39}}; {{John 6:35|John 6:35}}, {{John 6:48|48}}). In contrast, the Jewish leaders taught things that were wrong. Their false teaching spread everywhere, like yeast (or leaven) spreads through bread dough (see study note on Matt 16:11–12).

*Leaven* (or yeast) often symbolizes sin and evil (see {{Exodus 12:8|Exodus 12:8}}, {{Exodus 12:15|15}}; {{Leviticus 6:16-17|Leviticus 6:16–17}}; {{Galatians 5:9|Galatians 5:9}}). Here, it represents how deceptive teaching spreads.
*Caesarea Philippi *was about forty kilometers (twenty-five miles) north of Capernaum. It had many shrines (holy places) dedicated to Pan, the Roman god of nature.

Jesus asked his disciples who they believed he was. God had shown them that Jesus was more than a prophet. Jesus is God’s Son and the Messiah. He is Israel’s true King.

Jesus then taught the disciples that Israel’s King would suffer and die. Peter was angry and said that shouldn’t happen. Most Jews believed the messiah would be a warrior who would destroy all their enemies. Their biggest enemy at that time was the Roman government. But Jesus didn’t promise to destroy the Romans. Instead, he said that following him was like carrying a Roman cross and dying on it. He was talking about how hard it is to be fully committed to obeying God.

His followers must say no to everything that doesn’t honour God. Some of Jesus’ disciples would be killed for being faithful to him. But all who believe in Jesus and follow him will receive new life through his resurrection.

- Some, like Herod Antipas, thought Jesus was John the Baptist raised from the dead ({{Matthew 14:1-2|Matthew 14:1–2}}). 

- Others expected Elijah to return before the Messiah came ({{Matthew 11:14|11:14}}; {{Matthew 17:10-12|17:10–12}}; {{Malachi 3:1|Malachi 3:1}}; {{Malachi 4:5-6|4:5–6}}). 

- *Jeremiah or one of the prophets*: Some thought Jesus was Jeremiah or another prophet. Certain Jews believed Jeremiah would rise again (see *2 Maccabees* 15:13–16). Because Jesus spoke strongly on sensitive issues ({{Matthew 5:17|Matthew 5:17}}; {{Matthew 15:1-20|15:1–20}}), some thought he was Jeremiah. 

At this point, people did not yet understand that Jesus was the Messiah (God’s chosen one).

Peter acknowledges Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God" ({{Matthew 3:17|Matthew 3:17}}). This showed that God had opened Peter’s eyes through faith (see {{Matthew 11:25-27|11:25–27}}; {{Matthew 14:33|14:33}}; {{Matthew 27:54|27:54}}).

God revealed to Peter his plan for saving people through Jesus, the Messiah. This moment of revelation was key in showing God's will for humanity (see {{Galatians 1:16|Galatians 1:16}}; {{Galatians 3:23|3:23}}; {{Ephesians 3:5|Ephesians 3:5}}).

- In Greek, Peter’s name is *Petros*, which means “rock” or “stone.” When Jesus says, *on this rock* (Greek *petra*), he is making a play on words between Peter’s name (*Petros*) and the word for rock (*petra*).

Peter was the foundational "rock" because he was the first to confess Jesus as the Christ and was leader of the apostles. He was the "founding member" of the Church (see {{Ephesians 2:20-22|Ephesians 2:20–22}}; {{Revelation 21:14|Revelation 21:14}}). 

Some scholars think Jesus was talking about himself when he mentioned this rock. But it seems Jesus was referring to Peter or Peter's confession. However, it is clearly the church of Jesus, not of Peter. Jesus himself will build it. So, later church leaders do not need to get their authority from Peter. 

- Matthew is the only gospel writer who uses the term "church" (also {{Matthew 18:17|Matthew 18:17}}). Here, it means "the community of God’s people" rather than the expanded idea of an organized church. 

- *will not prevail against it*: The church will not be defeated by Satan's attacks (see {{Matthew 11:12|Matthew 11:12}}; {{Matthew 13:24-30|13:24–30}}, {{Matthew 13:36-43|36–43}}).

- *Keys* symbolize access to special knowledge that gives someone authority (see {{Matthew 13:16-17|Matthew 13:16–17}}; {{Matthew 23:13|23:13}}; {{Isaiah 22:22|Isaiah 22:22}}; {{Revelation 3:7|Revelation 3:7}}). 

- *bind … loose*: Jesus gave Peter (and later the rest of the twelve apostles, {{Matthew 18:18|Matthew 18:18}}) the authority to teach God's will as Jesus Christ revealed it ({{Matthew 13:52|13:52}}; {{Matthew 18:15-20|18:15–20}}; {{Matthew 23:2-12|23:2–12}}; {{Matthew 28:16-20|28:16–20}}). 

- *will be*: You could also translate this as *will have been. *This emphasizes that God’s sovereign decision comes first.

- This is the first of three times Jesus told his disciples that he would suffer. He said he would be betrayed, crucified, and killed (see also {{Matthew 17:22-23|Matthew 17:22–23}}; {{Matthew 20:18-19|20:18–19}}). Each of these predictions also taught a lesson about the cost of following him (see {{Matthew 16:24-27|16:24–27}}; {{Matthew 20:20-28|20:20–28}}). 

- The suffering of Jesus was part of God’s plan and was necessary for the Messiah (see {{Matthew 17:12|17:12}}).

Jesus was now officially recognized by his disciples as the Messiah. He then began to reveal a surprising part of his mission. He must suffer before entering his glory ({{Matthew 16:21-23|Matthew 16:21–23}}). Those who follow him will also face suffering ({{Matthew 16:24-28|16:24–28}}).
*began to rebuke Him*: Peter realized that Jesus was God's Messiah. But he did not understand that the Messiah had to suffer.

- Just as Satan tempted Jesus to take royal privileges without first going to the cross (see {{Matthew 4:8-10|Matthew 4:8–10}}), so now Jesus saw Peter’s words as stirred up by satanic forces.

- *a stumbling block: *This is something that causes a person to fall.

- *deny* … *take up *…* follow*: These three commands symbolize an extreme commitment. They mean confessing sins to God with humility, giving personal goals to God, and living by his will (see also {{Matthew 5:20|Matthew 5:20}}; {{Matthew 10:34-39|10:34–39}}; {{Matthew 18:1-5|18:1–5}}; {{Matthew 20:20-28|20:20–28}}). 

- *take up his cross:* This is a metaphor for devotion (see {{Luke 9:23|Luke 9:23}}). It is not necessarily a command to die for one's faith, though that is always a possibility for the disciples of Jesus ({{Matthew 5:10-12|Matthew 5:10–12}}; {{Matthew 10:21|10:21}}). 

- Matthew uses *follow* both literally (see {{Matthew 9:19|Matthew 9:19}}; {{Matthew 26:58|26:58}}) and as a metaphor. Metaphorically, it shows interest in a teacher ({{Matthew 4:25|4:25}}; {{Matthew 8:1|8:1}}, {{Matthew 8:10|10}}; {{Matthew 12:15|12:15}}; {{Matthew 14:13|14:13}}; {{Matthew 19:2|19:2}}; {{Matthew 20:29|20:29}}; {{Matthew 21:9|21:9}}) or personal loyalty to Jesus. This involves him summoning, a response to commit, and significant ongoing struggles ({{Matthew 4:20|4:20}}, {{Matthew 4:22|22}}; {{Matthew 8:19|8:19}}, {{Matthew 8:22-23|22–23}}; {{Matthew 9:9|9:9}}; {{Matthew 10:38|10:38}}; {{Matthew 16:24|16:24}}; {{Matthew 19:21|19:21}}, {{Matthew 19:27|27}}).

The disciples of Jesus need to give up control of their own lives, even being willing to suffer or die for him. Jesus promised that those who follow him in this way may suffer now, but at the final judgment God will show them to be right, clear away every false charge, and welcome them into his kingdom with honor (see {{1 Peter 2:23|1 Peter 2:23}}).
*His soul*: "Soul" and "life" ({{Matthew 16:25|Matthew 16:25}}) both translate the same Greek word *psuchē.* It refers to the essence or being of a person—the self.

The command to deny oneself and follow Jesus has its basis in the fact that Jesus will return to judge all people according to what they have done (see {{Matthew 19:28|Matthew 19:28}}; {{Matthew 24:29-31|24:29–31}}; {{Matthew 25:31|25:31}}; {{Psalm 62:12|Psalm 62:12}}; {{Proverbs 24:12|Proverbs 24:12}}).

Jesus took his three most trusted disciples up a mountain.

Peter, James and John saw Jesus’ glory as the Son of Man.

The change in his face and clothes showed them something. It showed them Jesus’ power and authority in the heavenly world.

Then Moses and Elijah both appeared. Their presence on the mountain was a sign. It was a sign that everything from Israel’s past led to Jesus.

Jesus is God’s Son. His work accomplishes all of God’s purposes.

Jesus told the three disciples not to tell others what they had seen on the mountain. They could only talk about it after Jesus was raised from the dead. That is when they would be able to understand what they had seen.

- *Peter, James, and John* later went with Jesus to Gethsemane ({{Matthew 26:37|Matthew 26:37}}; {{2 Peter 1:16-19|2 Peter 1:16–19}}). 

- We cannot know the exact location of this high mountain. The traditional site, Mount Tabor, is about 580 meters high (1,900 feet). It is not on the way if leaving from Caesarea Philippi ({{Matthew 16:13|Matthew 16:13}}) to go to Capernaum ({{Matthew 17:24|17:24}}). 

Mount Hermon is another option. It is about 2,800 meters high (9,200 feet) and located in Syria, about sixty-four kilometers (forty miles) north of Capernaum. Yet, it is improbable that “scribes” ({{Mark 9:14|Mark 9:14}}) would have gathered at the base of a mountain in non-Jewish territory. A likely location is Mount Meron, about 1,220 meters high (4,000 feet). It is located between Caesarea Philippi and Capernaum.

*He was transfigured*: In this moment, the inner and divine nature of Jesus, normally hidden, was now revealed. The three disciples were given a glimpse of his glory (see {{Exodus 34:29-35|Exodus 34:29–35}}; {{Psalm 104:2|Psalm 104:2}}; {{2 Corinthians 3:12-18|2 Corinthians 3:12–18}}; {{Revelation 1:16|Revelation 1:16}}). All of the disciples of Jesus will share in this glory one day ({{Matthew 13:43|Matthew 13:43}}).

Moses represents the law, and Elijah represents the prophets. They appeared as witnesses to Christ. Their presence showed that Jesus, the Son of God, fulfills everything written in the law and the prophets (see {{Matthew 5:17-20|Matthew 5:17–20}}; {{Matthew 11:2-6|11:2–6}}; {{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}).

*Three shelters* (Or* three tabernacles*): Peter probably thought the kingdom of heaven was about to arrive in full glory (compare {{Acts 1:6|Acts 1:6}}). He wanted to remember the moment by building shelters.

- *A bright cloud enveloped them:* In the Old Testament, a cloud often showed God’s presence with Israel during the time of Moses (see {{Exodus 24:15-18|Exodus 24:15–18}}; {{Exodus 25:8|25:8}}; {{Exodus 29:45-46|29:45–46}}; {{Exodus 40:34-38|40:34–38}}). 

- *My beloved Son*: This confirmed what Peter had already declared about Jesus ({{Matthew 16:16-17|Matthew 16:16–17}}). 

- The disciples were told to listen to Jesus because he is God’s Son. As a prophet, he reveals God’s will ({{Matthew 11:27|11:27}}; see {{Deuteronomy 18:15|Deuteronomy 18:15}}, {{Deuteronomy 18:18|18}}; {{Acts 3:22-23|Acts 3:22–23}}; {{Acts 7:37|7:37}}).

People often react this way when they experience God's glory (for example, {{Isaiah 6:5|Isaiah 6:5}}; {{Daniel 8:17|Daniel 8:17}}; {{Daniel 10:9|10:9}}, {{Daniel 10:15-19|15–19}}; {{Revelation 1:17|Revelation 1:17}}).
People could not fully understand Jesus until he completed his work, especially his death and resurrection.

Elijah’s appearance made the disciples ask about the belief that Elijah must return before the Messiah comes (see {{Malachi 4:5-6|Malachi 4:5–6}}). Jesus pointed to John the Baptist as the one who fulfilled that role. In doing so, he reminded them of the surprising truth that the Messiah must suffer, just as John, his forerunner, had also suffered ({{Matthew 14:3-12|Matthew 14:3–12}}).

The disciples were struggling. They had been looking for a messiah who would destroy the Romans.

The disciples had seen Jesus’ power over evil spiritual beings. So they believed he could make the nation of Israel strong again. They thought he would do this with force and power.

But when they tried to act based on this kind of faith, they failed. Jesus was troubled and concerned. He didn’t want them to do God’s work using force or their own strength. He wanted them to completely trust God. He wanted them to depend fully on God’s power to accomplish what God wanted done.

God can do anything. Through a fish he provided the money the disciples needed to pay their taxes.

Yet Jesus said that he would be killed. Death was part of how he would serve God and others. The disciples were confused and sad. This was a time of testing (test) for them.

*O unbelieving and perverse generation*: This phrase often describes moral corruption (see {{Deuteronomy 32:5|Deuteronomy 32:5}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:19-22|19–22}}). Jesus usually directed this exclamation at unbelieving Jewish crowds or leaders who refused to recognize God's presence in him (see {{Matthew 12:39|Matthew 12:39}}). But here the phrase sharply criticizes his disciples for not trusting in Jesus and his power to save and heal.

- Here, the phrase *so little faith* means the same as *no faith*. 

- *faith the size of a mustard seed*: This suggests that even a tiny amount of faith can help the disciples achieve great things ({{Matthew 21:21|Hebrews 21:21}}; compare {{1 Corinthians 13:2|1 Corinthians 13:2}}). It also suggests that if they let their faith increase (see {{Matthew 13:31-32|Matthew 13:31–32}}), they could act with strong belief.

- "Moving mountains" is a saying that means overcoming obstacles and achieving God's goals ({{Isaiah 40:4|Isaiah 40:4}}; {{Isaiah 49:11|49:11}}; {{Isaiah 54:10|54:10}}; {{1 Corinthians 13:2|1 Corinthians 13:2}}).
*be delivered*: See {{Matthew 20:18|Matthew 20:18}}; {{Matthew 26:14-16|26:14–16}}, {{Matthew 26:45-49|45–49}} to see how this prophecy came true.

- Every adult citizen of Israel had to pay the temple tax of one-half shekel. This was a coin weighing 4 grams. In the time of Jesus, priests and some rabbis did not pay this tax. 

- Peter spoke on behalf of the twelve apostles (see {{Matthew 10:2|Matthew 10:2}}).

As an obedient Jew, Jesus would have paid the tax every year, and he did pay it. The lesson Jesus wanted to teach was that as God's Son, he is greater than the temple ({{Matthew 12:5-6|Matthew 12:5–6}}). By this, he showed that a decisive break with the temple was coming (see {{Matthew 16:18-19|16:18–19}}; {{Matthew 21:33-46|21:33–46}}).

*At that time:* Matthew connects the disciples' questions to the earlier teaching about the temple. The disciples started to think their new freedom from Jewish authority gave them their own authority. 

Jesus had also spoken about special revelations ({{Matthew 11:25-27|Matthew 11:25–27}}; {{Matthew 13:11-17|13:11–17}}) and about leadership roles ({{Matthew 10:2-4|10:2–4}}; {{Matthew 19:28|19:28}}). This may have caused jealousy and arguments about power among the disciples. Their disputes may have centered on the importance of Peter ({{Matthew 17:25|17:25}}) or the special place of Peter, James, and John ({{Matthew 17:1-3|17:1–3}}).

This was the beginning of Jesus’ fourth long message. In it he talked about what it means to be important. He also talked about forgiving others.

In Jesus’ time, many people didn’t think children were complete human beings yet. But Jesus showed that children are very important. Children have many needs and must trust others to take care of them. Jesus said it’s a terrible thing to cause children to sin. It’s terrible to do that to anyone who is humble and trusting.

Jesus also taught that his disciples must become like little children in God’s kingdom. They must stop trying to be considered important. They must be humble and trust Jesus. This is what it means to be like a little one who believes in Jesus.

Yet the disciples were also leaders in God’s work. They weren’t to cause children or any of Jesus’ followers to sin. They were to be careful to teach the truth about God. Jesus was very serious about this. He talked about harming the body to avoid sin. He didn’t mean that people should actually hurt themselves. Jesus was talking in a way that made people listen to him. He wanted them to understand how important it was to follow God’s way of life.

This fourth major teaching in Matthew (see study note on Matthew 5:1–7:29) focuses on how people responded to the Messiah. The disciples accepted him, while the Jewish leaders and most people did not. As this division increased, Jesus taught his disciples about community life. 

To follow the standards of Jesus, a community should live with:

- humility ({{Matthew 18:1-5|18:1–5}}), 

- sensitivity ({{Matthew 18:6-9|18:6–9}}), 

- compassion ({{Matthew 18:10-14|18:10–14}}), 

- discipline ({{Matthew 18:15-18|18:15–18}}), and 

- forgiveness ({{Matthew 18:21-35|18:21–35}}). 

Like the other teachings, a closing statement ({{Matthew 19:1-2|19:1–2}}) connects to the next section.
*Like little children* means being humble ({{Matthew 18:4|Matthew 18:4}}). The disciples had been focused on status and ambition.
Jesus then talked about unity in the community. Welcoming a humble disciple of Jesus is the same as welcoming Jesus himself (see {{Matthew 10:40-42|Matthew 10:40–42}}).

- *Cause one … to stumble*: This means to lead believers to turn away from Christ, whether children or adults who have become “like children” in faith (see {{Matthew 18:3|Matthew 18:3}}). 

- The title *little ones* emphasizes their humility (see {{Matthew 5:3-12|5:3–12}}; {{Matthew 18:4|18:4}}; {{Matthew 19:13-15|19:13–15}}). 

- The thought of being drowned with a large millstone around the neck is terrifying. But Jesus warned that causing someone to lose faith will bring even greater suffering ({{Matthew 18:7|18:7}}; {{Matthew 26:24|26:24}}; {{Revelation 18:21|Revelation 18:21}}; {{Matthew 22:13|Matthew 22:13}}).
Jesus shifts his concern to the person. You must remove anything that leads you to sin (see {{Matthew 5:29-30|Matthew 5:29–30}}; {{Colossians 3:5-17|Colossians 3:5–17}}).

- *Do not look down on any of these:* This can happen by refusing to welcome them ({{Matthew 18:5-6|Matthew 18:5–6}}) or by not providing pastoral care when needed ({{Matthew 18:12-14|18:12–14}}; see {{Matthew 19:13-15|19:13–15}}). 

- *their angels*: See {{Matthew 4:5-7|Matthew 4:5–7}}; {{Hebrews 1:14|Hebrews 1:14}}.
Just as a shepherd works to find a lost sheep, we must not despise or ignore the “little ones” ({{Matthew 18:6|Matthew 18:6}}).

Humans are like sheep that are lost from God’s family.

God the Father sends his Son into the world to find them.

He is full of joy about each one who comes home.

God doesn’t want anyone to ever be apart from his love and life.
The shepherd's joy is the same as the Father's joy. The goal of pastoral care is to ensure God keeps all his sheep.

If another believer sins, love means we should talk to them privately and point out the wrong ({{Leviticus 19:17|Leviticus 19:17}}; {{Luke 17:3|Luke 17:3}}; {{Galatians 6:1|Galatians 6:1}}; {{1 Timothy 5:20|1 Timothy 5:20}}; {{Titus 3:10|Titus 3:10}}).
Resolving issues should be private at first and only made public if absolutely necessary.

Jesus described the kingdom of heaven as God’s household. It’s full of God’s children who are all brothers and sisters.

Jesus taught God’s children to deal with conflict, pray together and forgive one another. Two people who have a conflict must seek peace together with honesty and humility. If they can’t reach an agreement, they must ask others for help. People who refuse to stop harming others can’t stay in God’s family unless they change.

Jesus promised to be with his followers who pray together. He promised that God will answer their prayers.

Then Jesus told a story to answer Peter’s question about forgiving his brothers and sisters. God is like the king who showed great mercy to the servant and forgave him. But the servant who received mercy and forgiveness didn’t show mercy to the other servant. God’s children mustn’t be like that. They show they are grateful for God’s mercy when they forgive one another.

The community of believers should stay united and avoid conflicts. Members should seek reconciliation ({{Matthew 18:15-20|Matthew 18:15–20}}) and be ready to forgive ({{Matthew 18:21-35|18:21–35}}). Sometimes, strict discipline might be necessary ({{Matthew 18:17|18:17}}).

By requiring one or two others to be present, Jesus stopped slander and false accusations among the congregation (see {{John 8:17|John 8:17}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:1|2 Corinthians 13:1}}; {{1 Timothy 5:19|1 Timothy 5:19}}; {{Hebrews 10:28|Hebrews 10:28}}).

- The church is the local Christian community. 

- An unrepentant person (someone refusing to turn from sin) is to be treated as an outsider, like a lawbreaker. Excluding a person from fellowship (sometimes called excommunication) comes from the belief that God’s people must be holy ({{Acts 5:1-6|Acts 5:1–6}}; {{Romans 16:17|Romans 16:17}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:1-13|1 Corinthians 5:1–13}}; {{2 Corinthians 6:14-18|2 Corinthians 6:14–18}}; {{Galatians 5:7-12|Galatians 5:7–12}}; {{2 Thessalonians 3:14-15|2 Thessalonians 3:14–15}}). Sin harms fellowship with both other believers and with God. The goal is not revenge or control, but to restore the sinner to holiness and community ({{Matthew 18:10-15|Matthew 18:10–15}}; {{Galatians 6:1|Galatians 6:1}}; {{James 5:19-20|James 5:19–20}}).

*Bind … loose*: The privilege and authority Jesus gave to Peter ({{Matthew 16:19|Matthew 16:19}}) are here given to the church (or possibly to the twelve apostles, {{Matthew 18:1|18:1}}). The community's decisions, when they are in agreement with God's will, are eternally binding.
These sayings guide how to discipline and restore members in the community of disciples.
*Anything you ask for*: In the context of church discipline ({{Matthew 18:15-17|18:15–17}}), this means discipline must be done in a prayerful way.
Christ is present in the process of church discipline, so this process confirms God's decision.

Peter thought forgiving seven times was generous, but Jesus surprised him. A disciple should graciously forgive like God does, without limits and freely (see {{Matthew 18:10-14|Matthew 18:10–14}}). If someone does not forgive in this way, it shows they have not experienced God's forgiveness for themselves ({{Matthew 18:35|18:35}}; see {{Matthew 6:12|6:12}}).

*Seventy-seven times*: sus teaches that forgiveness should have no limit. His followers must forgive sincerely, not only in words but also in attitude and actions ({{Matthew 18:35|Matthew 18:35}}; see also {{Genesis 4:23-24|Genesis 4:23–24}}).
*Ten thousand talents*: The talent was the largest unit of currency, but its value changed over time. This debt was impossible to repay. This amount was more than all of Galilee's tax revenue.
*I will pay back everything: *the slave's promise to pay the huge debt emphasizes the king's great mercy and the slave's lack of forgiveness ({{Matthew 18:29-30|Matthew 18:29–30}}).
*A hundred denarii*: The first servant owed a debt about one million times larger than this amount owed to him.

- This is how God reacts to those who refuse to forgive ({{Matthew 18:35|Matthew 18:35}}). 

- *until he should repay all that he owed*: This means permanently, because he could never repay the debt.
*That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you*: Prison and torture ({{Matthew 18:34|Matthew 18:34}}) is a metaphor for hell (see {{Matthew 5:22|5:22}}).

The Pharisees were looking for ways to trap Jesus. They asked a question about divorce. The Law of Moses allowed people to get divorced. So they thought that God approved of divorce.

But Jesus taught them what God wanted for the world when he created it. Two people are made one when they get married. God wants them to always stay as one. They are like a picture of God’s faithful love. God helps some people to stay single. The important thing is to serve the kingdom of heaven whether married or single.

Then Jesus welcomed some children that his disciples were trying to send away. The children weren’t like the Pharisees who tried to trick Jesus. They simply trusted Jesus and received his blessing. He talked about them to explain the kingdom of heaven. His kingdom is for people who are humble and trust Jesus completely.
Jesus was traveling to Jerusalem ({{Matthew 19:1|Matthew 19:1}}; {{Matthew 20:29|20:29}}; {{Matthew 21:1|21:1}}). This was another chance to teach the disciples what it means to be his disciples.

There were two different opinions on when a man could divorce his wife: 

- One group of Pharisees, following Rabbi Shammai, believed divorce was only allowable for adultery or serious wrongdoing. 

- The other group, following Rabbi Hillel, thought a man could divorce his wife for any reason, even if she burned his dinner.

The Pharisees did not consider *all* of God's teachings. God intended marriage to be a permanent union (see {{Genesis 2:18-25|Genesis 2:18–25}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 7:10-16|1 Corinthians 7:10–16}}).
Since God created marriage as a union, people do not have the right to end it. Jesus confirmed that divorce should not happen.

*Why … did Moses order*: The Pharisees believed Jesus contradicted a command in the law (see {{Deuteronomy 24:1-4|Deuteronomy 24:1–4}}). But Moses allowed divorce only because of people's stubbornness. Jesus introduced the radical idea that what God permits is not always what he desires (see {{1 Corinthians 6:12|1 Corinthians 6:12}}). Divorce is never what God desires ({{Malachi 2:14-16|Malachi 2:14–16}}). It shows the brokenness of human sin.

- Jesus allows only one valid reason for a man to divorce: if his wife has been unfaithful (see {{Matthew 5:32|Matthew 5:32}}). For those who thought divorce was easy, Jesus emphasizes God's created order. Marriage is meant to last forever (see {{Mark 10:11-12|Mark 10:11–12}}). 

- *commits adultery*: This refers to a man who divorces his wife without a valid reason. If he remarries, it is the same as adultery. Jesus aims to reestablish that marriage is permanent.
This statement refers to what the disciples said in {{Matthew 19:10|Matthew 19:10}}.

- *Eunuchs* are men who cannot physically have children, either because of a birth defect or because they were made unable through surgery (castration). Jesus also used the word in a figurative way for those who choose not to marry (see {{Luke 14:26|Luke 14:26}}; {{Luke 18:29|18:29}}; {{1 Corinthians 7:7-8|1 Corinthians 7:7–8}}). 

- *for the sake of the kingdom of Heaven*: Jesus was not criticizing marriage. He meant that unmarried people often have more freedom for ministry (see {{1 Corinthians 7:25-35|1 Corinthians 7:25–35}}).

- Jesus would place his hands on others to bless them (see {{Luke 4:40|Luke 4:40}}; {{Luke 13:13|13:13}}; see also {{Genesis 48:14-15|Genesis 48:14–15}}; {{Acts 19:6|Acts 19:6}}). 

- The disciples tried to stop the parents from bringing children to Jesus. They wanted to protect him, but their action showed the wrong attitude toward children (see {{Matthew 18:5-6|Matthew 18:5–6}}, {{Matthew 18:10|10}}).

Doing good things or being rich doesn’t make someone part of God’s kingdom. Following Jesus allows people to share in God’s eternal life.

When people follow Jesus, they care about what God cares about. Jesus explained that it can be hard for rich people to care about God. This is because they often trust their money and not God.

The disciples were shocked at Jesus’ teachings. They were slowly realising that being faithful to Jesus was much harder than they thought. It meant that they would lose things that were important to them. Yet Jesus promised that they would receive so much more.

They would even have the wisdom and authority to judge the 12 tribes of Israel. That will happen when God makes all things new in the new creation.

- *Why do you ask Me:* as a Jew, the man should have known that God shows his standard of goodness in his commandments. The man's questions show he did not trust God's revealed will (also {{Matthew 19:20|Matthew 19:20}}). 

- *there is only One who is good*: The man might have thought he could be perfectly good on his own, but only God is the truly good. So, God is from where all goodness comes.

- *keep the commandments*: Jesus might be trying to show the man his own sinfulness by asking him to do the impossible. Or more probably, he is restating that good works are the clear measure of how true a person's faith is (see {{Matthew 7:13-27|7:13–27}}).

When Jesus told the man to *go, sell … come, follow*, Jesus revealed that the man had not truly followed the first of the Ten Commandments ({{Exodus 20:3|Exodus 20:3}}). His possessions (his wealth and security) had become his god (see {{Matthew 6:20|Matthew 6:20}}, {{Matthew 6:24|24}}; {{Matthew 13:44-46|13:44–46}}).

- Jesus teaches a lesson about discipleship from the rich man's sad refusal. It is difficult for the rich to humble themselves, admit their needs, and trust in God (see {{Matthew 5:3|Matthew 5:3}}; {{Luke 6:24|Luke 6:24}}; {{1 Timothy 6:9-10|1 Timothy 6:9–10}}). 

- *The kingdom of heaven* here means *eternal life* ({{Matthew 19:16-17|Matthew 19:16–17}}, {{Matthew 19:29|29}}) or *salvation* as a result of God's renewing work ({{Matthew 19:25-26|19:25–26}}).

- *Easier for a camel*: This analogy emphasizes how difficult it is *for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God*. Some manuscripts use a Greek word meaning *rope* (*kamilos*) instead of *camel* (*kamēlos*), a difference of only one letter. 

- *to pass through the eye of a needle*: This image suggests it is impossible for wealthy people to enter the kingdom of God. But the situation is not completely hopeless ({{Matthew 19:26-27|Matthew 19:26–27}}). See study note on Mark 10:25.
God's renewing grace is completely essential for the wealthy to be able to repent from making wealth an idol, give up their possessions if needed, and follow Jesus ({{Matthew 19:21|Matthew 19:21}}).

- *You … will also sit on twelve thrones*: The disciples will share in judging. This is a reversal, where those who are rich and powerful now will be judged by those who are humble and poor (see {{Matthew 19:30|Matthew 19:30}}). 

- *Judging* can mean both ruling with authority and condemning for wrongdoing (see {{Revelation 20:4|Revelation 20:4}}).

In Jesus’ time, workers would stand in the marketplace. They would stand with their tools and wait to be hired for the day. Even when there wasn’t enough work, the workers would keep waiting and hoping. They needed to earn money to buy food for that day.

Jesus told a story about this to teach his disciples about God’s grace. God is like the owner who paid each worker enough for that day’s needs. Those who had been hired early were jealous and angry. They were unhappy that those hired last received the same pay as they did. But the owner wanted to be generous with all the workers.

This is like God welcoming everyone who comes to him into his kingdom. They are all considered a full and equal part of God’s new family. They all depend on the King and Ruler who gives so freely.
This parable is like the parable of the lost son ({{Luke 15:11-32|Luke 15:11–32}}). In both, God shows grace to two groups, but one complains about unfair treatment.
Workers received their pay at the end of the day ({{Deuteronomy 24:14-15|Deuteronomy 24:14–15}}).

On his way to Jerusalem, Jesus worked hard to change how the disciples thought.

He made it clear that he was a leader who served others. He told them again that he would suffer and die. And then he would be raised from the dead.

The disciples still thought that God’s kingdom would be like human governments. Jesus invited them to share in a different kind of power. He wanted them to understand what honour and authority really mean in God’s kingdom.

True authority and honour aren’t based on the power to rule over others. They aren’t based on being more important than others. In God’s kingdom, power and authority are based on serving others.

Jesus then showed his disciples what it meant to serve others. He had deep concern for two blind men and healed them. True power and authority come only from following Jesus the Servant.
This mother's question seems to have come from her sons, as Jesus answered the sons instead of the mother (compare {{Mark 10:35-37|Mark 10:35–37}}).

Each time Jesus predicted his suffering in the Gospel of Matthew, he also gave teaching about what it means to be his disciple. These teachings showed that discipleship is shaped by Jesus own path of service and sacrifice (see {{Matthew 16:24-28|Matthew 16:24–28}}; {{Matthew 17:24-18:5|17:24–18:5}}). This teaching called the Messiah's disciples to imitate his service and sacrifice.

Jesus had already promised positions of authority in God’s kingdom to the disciples ({{Matthew 19:28|Matthew 19:28}}). The request of the two brothers came from selfish desire to be important, without concern for the suffering the Messiah would soon face (see {{Matthew 23:6|Matthew 23:6}}; {{Luke 14:7-11|Luke 14:7–11}}).

The* cup* refers to the duty duty, calling, and destiny of Jesus (see {{Matthew 26:39|Matthew 26:39}}; {{John 18:11|John 18:11}}; also {{Psalm 75:8|Psalm 75:8}}; {{Isaiah 51:17|Isaiah 51:17}}, {{Isaiah 51:22|22}}; {{Revelation 16:19|Revelation 16:19}}).
*You will indeed*: James eventually died for his faith ({{Acts 12:2|Acts 12:2}}). John suffered severe persecution ({{Acts 4:3|Acts 4:3}}; {{Acts 5:40|5:40}}; {{Revelation 1:9|Revelation 1:9}}).

*The ten … they were indignant:* This shows that selfish ambition was not only in James and John. The other disciples also struggled with it (see also {{Matthew 21:15|Matthew 21:15}}; {{Matthew 26:8|26:8}}; {{Luke 13:14|Luke 13:14}}).

Rulers who do not know God often desire power and control. But those who follow the Son of Man should not act this way ({{Matthew 18:1-5|Matthew 18:1–5}}; {{Matthew 19:13-15|19:13–15}}; {{Matthew 23:1-12|23:1–12}}).

Often the word *slave* is a metaphor that describes a disciple's submissive relationship to their master ({{Matthew 8:9|Matthew 8:9}}; {{Matthew 10:24-25|10:24–25}}; {{Matthew 24:45-51|24:45–51}}; {{Matthew 25:14-30|25:14–30}}). The disciples of Jesus serve others, following his example (for example, {{John 13:1-17|John 13:1–17}}).

- The phrase* the Son of Man … come*: This expression suggests that Jesus already existed before his birth on earth. It points back to Daniel’s vision of the Son of Man coming from heaven to receive authority and glory (see {{Daniel 7:13-14|Daniel 7:13–14}}). 

- *as a ransom for many: *Jesus said he would freely give his life as a payment to rescue many people. His death brought freedom from the power and penalty of sin (see {{Matthew 26:26-29|Matthew 26:26–29}}; {{Isaiah 53:10-12|Isaiah 53:10–12}}; {{Romans 3:24|Romans 3:24}}). In this way, he bought them out of slavery to sin (see {{Galatians 5:1|Galatians 5:1}}).

The blind men’s expression of faith in the Son of David was an acknowledgment of Jesus as the Messiah (see {{Matthew 21:9|Matthew 21:9}}; {{Matthew 22:42|22:42}}; {{2 Samuel 7:12-16|2 Samuel 7:12–16}}).
